mcq.explanation: `git init` initializes a local Git repository by creating the hidden `.git` directory in the current folder.
mcq.distractors: `git boot`, `git create` and `git start` are not Git commands.

mcq.explanation: `git add` stages a file: it copies the current content into the index so it will be part of the next commit.
mcq.distractors: `git fetch` downloads remote data, `git log` shows history and `git push` uploads commits.

mcq.explanation: `git commit` records staged changes as a new commit (snapshot) with a message, author and parent.
mcq.distractors: `git status` and `git diff` only inspect changes, and `git clone` copies a repository.

mcq.explanation: `git status` shows the current working tree state: the branch, staged changes, unstaged changes and untracked files.
mcq.distractors: `git branch -d` deletes a branch, `git gc` cleans up the object database and `git tag -d` deletes a tag.

mcq.explanation: `git branch feature` creates a new branch called feature at the current commit (without switching to it; `git switch -c feature` creates and switches).
mcq.distractors: `git reset` moves the current branch, `git commit` records changes and `git push` uploads; none of them create branches.

mcq.explanation: `git merge <branch>` integrates another branch into the current branch, with a fast-forward or a merge commit.
mcq.distractors: `git fetch` only downloads, `git clean` deletes untracked files and `git stash` shelves uncommitted changes.

mcq.explanation: `git clone` copies a repository to a local directory, including its full history, and sets `origin` as the remote.
mcq.distractors: Clone does not delete branches, rename commits or touch the operating system.

mcq.explanation: A pull request is used for reviewing and discussing changes before merge: teammates see the diff, comment, run CI checks and approve.
mcq.distractors: Docker layers, Kubernetes pods and VPCs are unrelated to code review.

mcq.explanation: `.gitignore` lists which untracked paths Git should ignore (e.g. `node_modules/`, `.env`, build output). Files already tracked are not affected until you `git rm --cached` them.
mcq.distractors: Access control is configured on GitHub, the author comes from `user.name`/`user.email`, and remotes are set with `git remote`.

mcq.explanation: `git push` uploads local commits to a remote branch, e.g. `git push origin main`.
mcq.distractors: `git pull` downloads and merges, `git diff` compares changes and `git show` displays a commit.

labs.modelAnswer:
mkdir todo-app && cd todo-app
git init -b main

# commit 1: README
echo '# Todo App' > README.md
echo 'A tiny CLI todo list.' >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m 'Add README with project description'

# commit 2: application code
echo 'print("todo app")' > app.py
git add app.py
git commit -m 'Add initial app entry point'

# commit 3: ignore file
printf '__pycache__/\n.env\n' > .gitignore
git add .gitignore
git commit -m 'Ignore Python cache and env files'

git log --oneline

# push to GitHub (create an empty repo named todo-app first)
git remote add origin git@github.com:<your-username>/todo-app.git
git push -u origin main
labs.explanation: Tests the basic Git workflow: init, stage, commit, connect a remote and push. Look for at least three separate commits with meaningful, imperative messages (not 'update'), and `git push -u origin main` so the local branch tracks the remote. Verify with `git log --oneline` and by checking the repository page on GitHub.

labs.modelAnswer:
git switch main
git pull
git switch -c feature/add-health-endpoint

# implement the change
echo 'def health(): return "ok"' >> app.py
git diff                      # review locally before staging
git add app.py
git commit -m 'Add health endpoint'
git push -u origin feature/add-health-endpoint

# open the Pull Request (web UI or GitHub CLI)
gh pr create --base main --head feature/add-health-endpoint --title 'Add health endpoint' --body 'Adds a simple health check.'
gh pr diff                    # review the diff (or the 'Files changed' tab on GitHub)
gh pr merge --merge --delete-branch

# update local main
git switch main
git pull
git log --oneline --graph
labs.explanation: Tests the feature-branch and Pull Request workflow used by most teams. Verify the change was made on a separate branch, pushed with upstream tracking, reviewed as a diff in the PR (Files changed tab or `gh pr diff`) and merged into main, then that local main was updated with `git pull`. Deleting the merged branch keeps the repo tidy.

labs.modelAnswer:
git switch main
echo 'greeting = "Hello"' > config.py
git add config.py && git commit -m 'Add greeting config'

# branch A edits line 1
git switch -c feature-a
echo 'greeting = "Hello from A"' > config.py
git commit -am 'Change greeting on feature-a'

# main edits the same line
git switch main
echo 'greeting = "Hello from main"' > config.py
git commit -am 'Change greeting on main'

# merge -> conflict
git merge feature-a
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in config.py
git status                    # shows 'both modified: config.py'
cat config.py
# <<<<<<< HEAD
# greeting = "Hello from main"
# =======
# greeting = "Hello from A"
# >>>>>>> feature-a

# resolve: edit the file, keep the final line, remove the conflict markers
echo 'greeting = "Hello from main and A"' > config.py
git add config.py
git commit -m 'Merge feature-a, resolve greeting conflict'

git log --oneline --graph --all
labs.explanation: Tests understanding of how merge conflicts arise (both branches changed the same line since their common ancestor) and how to resolve them: edit the file, delete the `<<<<<<<`, `=======` and `>>>>>>>` markers, `git add` to mark it resolved, then commit. `git log --oneline --graph` should show the two diverging commits joined by a merge commit.
